name: Nāth tradition (Nātha Siddhas; Nāth / Kānphaṭa Yogīs)

tradition.text: Ādinātha (Śiva) is the first Nāth; Matsyendra received the teaching from him; Gorakṣa is held to be immortal and to have appeared in each of the four ages

scholarly.text: Matsyendra c. 9th–10th c. (honoured by Abhinavagupta, Tantrāloka 1.7); Gorakṣa c. 11th–13th c.; the order with its twelve panths is consolidated later (c. 15th–18th c.)

transmissions_received.what: Matsyendra's Kaula teaching: the body as the locus of the divine, the Kula/Akula, the centres of the body, the nectar of the moon, the conquest of death and the yoginīs
transmissions_received.evidence: Kaulajñānanirṇaya colophons name Macchaghnapāda/Matsyendra as its bringer; Nāth lists begin with Ādinātha and Matsyendra (HYP 1.5).

transmissions_received.what: the ascetic style of the skull-bearing and ash-smeared Śaiva ascetics (earrings, ash, cremation-ground associations)
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis only (the tradition does not claim Kāpālika descent).

transmissions_received.what: shared siddha figures and songs (Jālandhara, Kāṇha, Cauraṅgī, Mīna, Virūpa, Carpaṭi)
transmissions_received.evidence: overlap of the Nāth and Buddhist eighty-four siddha lists (Varṇaratnākara; Abhayadatta); see brw:natha-mahasiddha.

transmissions_given.what: the haṭha corpus attributed to Gorakṣa and the lineage of Nāth siddhas at the head of the Haṭhapradīpikā (1.4–9)
Nāth initiation passed through Gahinīnāth to Nivṛttināth and Jñāneśvar (Jñāneśvarī 6.291; closing lineage ovīs of ch. 18)
the vocabulary of sahaja, śūnya, the unstruck sound, the tenth door and reversed speech (ulaṭbāṃsī) used by Kabīr and other Sants
Korakkar (Gorakṣa) and Macchamuni (Matsyendra) counted among the eighteen Tamil Siddhars
the cult of Matsyendranātha as Karuṇāmaya / Buṅga-dyaḥ in the Kathmandu valley (mutual; see dsp:identity-of-matsyendra)
regional Nāth saints and householder Jogī communities

distinctive_positions: The body (piṇḍa) contains the whole cosmos (brahmāṇḍa); liberation is realised in and through the body.
The goal is sahaja-samādhi / samarasa: the mind seeing the mind, the stilling of breath and mind in the void (śūnya) beyond the pairs (AmŚ 54; GŚ 94).
Perfection of the body (kāya-siddhi): an adamantine, deathless siddha body; conquest of death and time (kāla-vañcana) through retaining bindu and the moon's nectar.
Reversal (ulṭā sādhana): turning the downward flows of breath, bindu and mind upward to the head.
The guru is indispensable; the teaching passes ear to ear and is kept secret from the untested.
Rejection of caste, image-worship, pilgrimage, fasting and Vedic ritual as means to liberation for the knower (Akulavīra A.43–46; Gorakh Bānī).
Moderation and restraint (saṃyam), the 'middle way' of the yogī (Gorakh Bānī).
Distinctive order: split-ear initiation (kān-phaṛāī), earrings (darśan / mudrā), the nād horn on the selī thread, the dhūnī fire, the greeting 'ādeś', burial (samādhi) of yogīs rather than cremation.
Siddhis are signs, not the goal; the knower does not grasp them (Akulavīra B.83–84).
summary: The Nāth tradition traces itself to Ādinātha (Śiva), Matsyendranātha and Gorakṣanātha and to the nine Nāths and eighty-four Siddhas. It joins the Kaula teaching of Matsyendra's Yoginīkaula with the body-centred yoga later called haṭha, aiming at sahaja, the samarasa of Śiva and Śakti, liberation while living and the perfected, deathless body. Its ascetics (Kānphaṭa yogīs) are organised in twelve panths with monasteries from Gorakhpur and Tilla Jogian to Kadri and Nepal; its vernacular sayings (Gorakh Bānī) and sagas (Gopīcand, Bharthari, Mayanāmatī, the rescue of Matsyendra) shaped Sant, Vārkarī and folk religion across India.
notes: family 'vedic' follows the coverage-map grouping (A7, Śaiva lineages); it does not settle the tradition's own rejection of Vedic ritual authority (see dsp:natha-varna-and-ritual) nor its overlap with the Buddhist Mahāsiddhas (C; brw:natha-mahasiddha).

name: Aghora (Aghor panth; Aghorī and Aughaṛ ascetics)
regions: Varanasi (Kīnārām Sthal / Krīm Kuṇḍ at Śivālā; Parāo)

tradition.text: Kīnārām, born Vikrama 1658 (1601 CE) at Rāmgaṛh near Varanasi, lived to 1771 CE; Dattātreya is the ādiguru

scholarly.text: the Kīnārāmī lineage is attested from the 18th c.; any continuity with the medieval Kāpālikas is a scholarly hypothesis

transmissions_received.what: Dattātreya as ādiguru; Girnar as the place of Kīnārām's vision
Kīnārām's first (Vaiṣṇava) initiation under Śivarām and the Rāma-devotional language of his works (Rāmgītā, Rāmrasāl)
transmissions_received.evidence: the tradition's account; titles of Kīnārām's works.

transmissions_received.what: cremation-ground practice, skull bowl, transgression of purity rules
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis; not the tradition's own account.

transmissions_given.what: the Aghora lineage re-shaped toward social service (1961 onward)

distinctive_positions: Non-discrimination (abheda): nothing is to be shunned as impure; the aghora (the 'not-terrible') Śiva is present in what is feared and loathed.
Freedom from the eight fetters — disgust, doubt, fear, shame, loathing, family, conduct and caste (the Kaula list, Kulārṇava 13.90) — is the mark of the free one.
The cremation ground (śmaśāna) is the place of practice; the skull bowl (khappar) is carried.
The guru is Śiva; the lineage descends from Dattātreya through Kālūrām and Kīnārām.
The ultimate is named also as Rām / nirguṇa (Kīnārām's works); the state sought is sahaja and unmanī.
Recent teachers (Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām) direct Aghora toward service of the sick and outcaste and rejection of caste distinctions.
summary: Aghora is the lineage of Śaiva ascetics centred on Bābā Kīnārām's seat at Krīm Kuṇḍ in Varanasi, who trace their teaching to Dattātreya through Bābā Kālūrām. Its ascetics practise in the cremation ground and cultivate non-discrimination (abheda), overcoming disgust, fear and the other fetters. Kīnārām's Hindi works (Vivekasār, Rāmgītā, Rāmrasāl, Gītāvalī) join this with devotion to Rām as the attributeless; in the twentieth century Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām founded the Śrī Sarveśvarī Samūh and turned the lineage toward service. Practice details are secret and only summarised here.
notes: family 'vedic' follows the coverage-map grouping (A7, Śaiva lineages); it does not settle the tradition's own rejection of Vedic ritual authority (see dsp:natha-varna-and-ritual (Aghora shares the Nāth position)) nor its overlap with the Buddhist Mahāsiddhas (C; brw:natha-mahasiddha). Tradition's dates for Kīnārām are recorded as the tradition gives them; they are not independently confirmed.

name: Yoginī Kaula (Yoginīkaula) of Matsyendra
alt_names: Siddha Kaula (as a stage in the Kaulajñānanirṇaya's account)
Matsyodara (the Kali-age form of the Kaula)

tradition.text: the Kaula descended in each age: as Jñānanirṇiti, Mahat, Siddhāmṛta and, in the Kali age, as Matsyodara 'from the fish's belly' (KJN 16.47–48)

scholarly.text: the oldest Kaulajñānanirṇaya manuscript (Nepal) was assigned by its editor to c. the 11th c.; the teaching is usually placed c. 9th–11th c.

transmissions_given.what: Matsyendra's Kaula teaching and his place at the head of the Nāth lineage
one of the Kaula currents named in later Kaula lists

distinctive_positions: The true liṅga is the body-liṅga, worshipped with eight inner flowers (non-harming, sense-restraint, compassion, feeling, patience, conquest of anger, meditation, knowledge) (KJN 3.24–29).
One whose tendency (vāsanā) rests in the body belongs to the Kula; one whose tendency is outward is a bound 'animal' (paśu) (KJN 3.31).
Śiva is not without Śakti nor Śakti without Śiva (KJN 17.8); the self is guru, siddha, disciple and Śiva (KJN 11.26).
Nectar-meditations conquer death and old age; eleven centres of the body grant powers (KJN 5).
The teaching is given only to a tested, devoted disciple, ear to ear (KJN 5.35; 6.9; 17.10–11).
The Kaula path is of two kinds, made (kṛtaka) and innate (sahaja); the aroused kuṇḍalī is 'made', the innate abides in samarasa (Akulavīra B.43).
Kaula rites with meat, wine, fish, sexual union and bodily substances are taught (summary only; restricted) (KJN 8; 11; 18).
summary: The Yoginīkaula is the Kaula current that the Kaulajñānanirṇaya says Macchaghnapāda (Matsyendra) brought down from Candradvīpa and that was 'in every house of the yoginīs' in Kāmarūpa (KJN 22.10). Its texts, edited by P. C. Bagchi, teach the body-liṅga, the centres and nectar of the body, the conquest of death, the Akula beyond all distinctions and the secrecy of the Kaula; the Nāth tradition places Matsyendra at its head.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U21 (Matsyendra's own Kaula school); U24 owns lin:kaula.

name: Śrī Sarveśvarī Samūh (Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām's Aghora organisation)
alt_names: Avadhūt Bhagavān Rām Kuṣṭh Sevāśram (its service institution)

transmissions_received.evidence: Bhagavān Rām's initiation in the Aghora line (tradition's account)

distinctive_positions: Aghora expressed as service (especially of leprosy patients) and as rejection of caste and social evils, open to householders; the cremation-ground practices are not required of lay members.
summary: A recent Aghora organisation founded by Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām at Varanasi, known for its leprosy service and for presenting Aghora as naturalness and service rather than as spectacular ascetic practice.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U21. Founding year and institutional names as commonly reported; to be sourced.
